source.title: Evaluating the Interpretability of Sparse Autoencoders with Concept Annotations
source.authors: Jonas Klotz; C. F. Dantas; P. Jain; Diego Marcos; B. Demir

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates SAE feature alignment and perturbation responses in CLIP and DINOv2 vision encoders, extending sparse-feature evaluation to vision rather than testing the original toy-network setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own latent-to-concept matching and targeted-perturbation results. The cited claims about neurons being polysemantic and superposed, and the cited results from prior SAE studies, are background rather than this study's results. Matching scores, TAPAScores, and their trends are included; training statistics that do not bear on the claim are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on CLIP and DINOv2 vision-encoder embeddings. It measures how well SAE latents match human-annotated concepts against untrained and random baselines and a supervised probe bound. It also tests whether matched latents respond to single-attribute image edits. These results bear on whether dictionary features are complete, reliable units (V5) in a new setting. Much of the paper validates its own metrics; those rows are unlinked.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add three points the authors stress: only their matching and TAPAScore pass sanity checks separating trained from untrained or random SAEs, while FMS, MS and CKNNA fail; they recommend FBMP F0.5 (k=3) with TAPAScore as the default protocol; and overcompleteness can reduce perturbation alignment, a loss of interpretability, with moderate dictionary sizes and K in {16, 32} giving the best trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse autoencoders on pretrained vision-model embeddings and evaluates annotated-concept matching and image-perturbation responses; it does not reproduce the original toy-network feature-geometry experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with dataset, SAE variant, dictionary size, activation sparsity K, matching criterion, and backbone (CLIP versus DINOv2).

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on CLIP and DINOv2 class-token embeddings recover latents aligned with annotated bird attributes and COCO objects above an untrained-SAE baseline. These latents respond to targeted image edits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A V4 analogue for vision encoders: sparse, concept-aligned features recoverable by a dictionary exist in vision transformer embeddings.

record.problems: Results for many central comparisons are described qualitatively from figures rather than reported as numerical values in the text. Evaluation depends on human-annotated concept quality and granularity, and the authors note that annotation errors can affect matching and TAPAScore. The synthetic perturbation datasets are generated with an image-editing model and curated; the paper reports classifier performance gaps between original and synthetic images.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed metric comparisons against FMS, MS, and CKNNA, and matching comparisons against NN-OMP, were omitted because they primarily evaluate the proposed evaluation metrics rather than directly bearing on the listed claim versions. Additional per-configuration figure trends in Figs. S25–S31 were summarized where the text states the result.

untested.parts: Toy models, sparsity-dependent transition, and the geometry of superposed features.
All of it in LLMs. Only vision encoders (CLIP ViT-L/14, DINOv2 ViT-S/14) are studied. Neuron-level spreading of features is not measured.
Cross-run stability and canonicality across seeds, methods or models. Completeness is tested only against annotated concepts and one probe bound.

missing.what: FBMP run with k=20 on CUB. About 50% of attributes use at most 5 latents; few need more than 10. The authors read large coalitions as concepts the SAE did not learn well. This bears on V5 single-unit features.

Qualitative failures. A rare concept (purple underparts) gets no dedicated latent. Latents capture colour without part localization, and some latents conflate tennis context with sports ball. These bear on V5 completeness.
missing.locator: Sec. S5; Figs. S21, S23, S24

missing.what: Matching scores of untrained SAEs rise steadily with dictionary size. This inflates raw matching and motivates ΔMATCHScore; it is a baseline needed to read r1–r3.

record.verdict_notes: This is mainly an evaluation-methods paper; rows on metric validation (r9, r10, r16, r18) are unlinked. V4 links were removed because V4 names LLMs and the study uses vision encoders. The vision-encoder recovery result is placed under fits_no_version; a curator might instead treat vision as a T3 setting for V4. Most results are read from figures; few numbers are given in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity and importance as determinants of superposition geometry, nearly orthogonal overlapping directions, and the proposed sparsity-dependent transition.

Whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by limited network capacity, whether important features receive dedicated dimensions, and whether less important features share dimensions. SAE dictionary size and activation sparsity are varied, but the study does not test this neuron-level account.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure, and whether polysemanticity alone is evidence of superposition.
The study tests SAE recovery of human-annotated concepts in vision encoders, not LLMs or the claim that LLM activations spread features across neurons.
The study evaluates concept alignment and targeted responses, but does not establish cross-run stability or that SAE features are canonical units across methods or models.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional subspaces.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Match binarized SAE activations to human-annotated CUB attributes using FBMP and compare with one-to-one F1 matching.

conditions.value: FBMP, k=3, compared with one-to-one F1, k=1

rows.value: FBMP consistently outperforms one-to-one matching across all four SAE variants; all SAE variants remain well below the supervised linear-probe upper bound.
rows.note: The paper describes the results across variants and dictionary sizes rather than reporting the plotted values in text. The results show recoverable concept alignment, but not complete recovery of the attribute information present in the embeddings.
rows.check: Partly a comparison of the study's own FBMP against one-to-one matching. It bears on V5 only in that concepts need coalitions of latents, not single latents. V4 link removed: vision encoders are not the LLMs V4 names.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Match binarized SAE activations to human-annotated COCO object labels using FBMP and compare with one-to-one F1 matching.

conditions.value: FBMP, k=3, compared with one-to-one F1, k=1

rows.value: FBMP consistently outperforms one-to-one matching across all four SAE variants; FBMP F0.5 achieves the highest scores overall.
rows.note: The authors report higher matching scores than on CUB and attribute this to the smaller, higher-level, more semantically distinct concept set.
rows.check: Same as r1: mainly a comparison of the study's own matching method. V4 link removed (not LLMs).

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Compare SAE latent-to-concept matching with a supervised linear-probe upper bound.
rows.measure: F1 matching score versus thresholded per-attribute linear-probe score
rows.value: All SAE variants remain well below the linear-probe upper bound; the authors state that only part of the attribute information in the embeddings is recovered as individual latents.
rows.note: Supports the presence of recoverable concept-aligned latents while limiting claims of completeness.
rows.check: V4 link removed (vision encoder, not LLM). The probe-bound gap shows incomplete recovery; it is CLIP-only in the main text.

rows.operation_detail: Measure matched latents' signed responses to single-attribute image perturbations.
rows.value: For BatchTopK and Matryoshka, TAPAScore closely mirrors the matching-score pattern.
rows.note: The paper describes the correspondence qualitatively; the figure contains the plotted values.
rows.check: V4 link removed. Qualitative only; TAPAScore values are in Fig. 5, not the text.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Measure matched latents' signed responses to single-attribute image perturbations.
rows.baseline: Matching-score trend for the same configurations
rows.value: Matching scores increase with dictionary size while TAPAScore peaks early and then degrades sharply.
rows.note: The authors say larger TopK dictionaries improve statistical alignment without necessarily encoding concepts that are causally valid.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Measure matched latents' signed responses to single-attribute image perturbations.
rows.value: FBMP TAPAScores fluctuate around a stable level across dictionary sizes; one-to-one TAPAScore declines beyond dictionary size 512.
rows.note: The outcome depends on the matching criterion.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Measure matched latents' signed responses to object-removal image perturbations.
rows.baseline: Matching-score trend for the same configurations
rows.value: TAPAScore follows the matching trend up to dictionary sizes 512–1024, then declines for larger dictionaries while matching continues to improve or saturate.
rows.note: The authors describe the decline as evidence that overcompleteness can degrade perturbation alignment despite improved matching quality.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Fig. 6 discussion; JumpReLU decline starts at 4096.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Measure matched latents' signed responses to object-removal image perturbations.
rows.baseline: Other SAE variants' trends as described in the same analysis
rows.value: FBMP F0.5 matching continues to improve beyond dictionary size 1024, reaching its maximum at 2048 before plateauing; the authors describe Matryoshka's TAPAScore pattern as different from the declining variants.
rows.note: The paper reports lower overall Matryoshka scores than the other SAE types.
rows.check: V4 link removed. Baseline should read: Matryoshka's own matching trend; its overall scores are lower than the other variants'.

source_check.correct: The Section 4.2 trend concerns Matryoshka TAPAScore under FBMP F0.5 (k=3): improvement beyond 1024, maximum at 2048, then a plateau. Baseline for matching-versus-perturbation comparison: Matryoshka's own matching-score trend. Overall Matryoshka scores are lower than other SAE variants.
source_check.problem: The row attributes the perturbation-score trend to matching and assigns the wrong baseline for the within-variant comparison.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Measure Pearson correlation between latent-to-concept matching and targeted perturbation alignment across SAE configurations.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between matching score and TAPAScore
rows.value: Positive correlation across all criteria; FBMP variants outperform one-to-one matching, and FBMP F0.5 has the highest correlation.
rows.note: Numerical correlation coefficients are not stated in the prose.
rows.check: Correlation between two of the study's own metrics. This validates the metrics and says nothing on whether SAE features are the model's units.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Measure Pearson correlation between latent-to-concept matching and targeted perturbation alignment across SAE configurations.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between matching score and TAPAScore
rows.value: Correlations are weaker overall; FBMP variants yield near-zero correlations, while one-to-one F1 yields a negative correlation.
rows.note: The authors associate the weaker relationship with matching continuing to improve while TAPAScore declines at larger dictionary sizes.

rows.subject: DINOv2 (ViT-S-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Match binarized SAE activations to human-annotated concepts.
rows.value: FBMP consistently outperforms one-to-one matching across all four variants; the one-to-one scores remain low across dictionary sizes.
rows.note: BatchTopK peaks at 512; Matryoshka peaks at 256, declines sharply at 512, then partially recovers; TopK broadly increases up to 2048; JumpReLU rises steadily and reaches its highest ΔMATCHScores at 4096.
rows.check: Partly a comparison of the study's own matching method. V4 link removed.

rows.subject: DINOv2 (ViT-S-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Match binarized SAE activations to human-annotated COCO object labels.
rows.value: Results largely mirror CLIP: FBMP consistently outperforms one-to-one matching and the relative ordering of matching criteria is preserved. JumpReLU is close to zero at dictionary sizes 128 and 256, then approaches the other variants from size 512 onward.
rows.note: The authors say absolute score differences between SAE variants are smaller on this dataset.
rows.check: Partly a comparison of the study's own matching method. V4 link removed.

rows.subject: DINOv2 (ViT-S-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Measure matched latents' responses to single-attribute image perturbations.
rows.value: Degradation at larger dictionary sizes is less pronounced than in CLIP results. BatchTopK is comparatively stable; TopK peaks at 256–512 and then decreases; JumpReLU peaks at 256–512 before a moderate decline; Matryoshka improves with dictionary size and reaches its highest values at the largest sizes.
rows.note: The outcome varies by SAE variant and backbone.

rows.subject: DINOv2 (ViT-S-14 backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Measure matched latents' responses to object-removal image perturbations.
rows.baseline: CLIP results for the corresponding setting
rows.value: TAPAScore is more stable across dictionary sizes than in the CLIP results, with less pronounced divergence between matching and perturbation alignment and only a mild decline at the largest sizes.
rows.note: The authors state that backbone choice influences the degree to which overcompleteness reduces causal alignment.

source_check.locator_found: Section S6.2, Fig. S26 bottom-row discussion.

rows.subject: CLIP (ViT-L-14 backbone)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained embeddings; SAE untrained or activations randomized
rows.operation_detail: Compare trained SAE metrics with an untrained TopK SAE and random activations.

conditions.value: untrained TopK SAE and random activations

rows.baseline: Trained SAEs, aggregated over dictionary sizes and SAE variants
rows.value: MATCHScores show clear absolute decreases for untrained and random conditions; TAPAScore drops to near zero for both conditions on both datasets.
rows.note: The result supports the paper's claim that its matching measures and TAPAScore distinguish trained SAE representations from these controls.
rows.check: State 'absent' is misframed. Trained SAEs score well above the untrained and random controls, i.e. concept alignment is present. This is also a metric sanity check, and it is CLIP only.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5: trained SAEs outperform untrained/random controls in semantic matching and perturbation alignment; this sanity check does not establish complete, stable, canonical units.
source_check.problem: Passing metric sanity checks does not establish the stronger V5 effect.

rows.subject: SAEs trained on CLIP and DINOv2 embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Measure the average absolute change in matched latents for attributes untouched by image perturbations.
rows.value: synCUB: All 0.21 ± 0.04; TopK 0.18 ± 0.05; BatchTopK 0.24 ± 0.03; Matryoshka 0.24 ± 0.02; JumpReLU 0.20 ± 0.02. synCOCO: All 0.12 ± 0.01; TopK 0.12 ± 0.01; BatchTopK 0.12 ± 0.01; Matryoshka 0.12 ± 0.01; JumpReLU 0.11 ± 0.01.
rows.uncertainty: Values are reported as mean ± std over dictionary sizes.
rows.note: The study describes these as low absolute drift and uses them to argue that high TAPAScores are not explained by unselective drift. The table does not break these results down by backbone.
rows.check: Δstay is a leakage check validating TAPAScore, not a result on SAE features as units. No baseline is given.

rows.subject: TopK SAEs trained on CLIP embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Vary the activation sparsity K and measure concept matching and perturbation alignment.
rows.value: On CUB, ΔMATCHScore peaks at K ∈ {16, 32} and declines sharply at larger K. On COCO, matching is stable for K ≤ 32 before degrading. synCOCO TAPAScore peaks at K=32; synCUB TAPAScore is highest at small sparsity levels, peaking at K=16 for FBMP F0.25.
rows.note: The authors conclude that K ∈ {16, 32} gives the best trade-off between statistical and causal alignment.

rows.subject: SAEs trained on CLIP embeddings
rows.operation_detail: Compare FBMP with naive top-k F1 matching as coalition size increases.
rows.value: FBMP matches or outperforms naive matching at every tested coalition size. For Matryoshka on COCO at k=10, the naive score is 0.08 at d=256 and 0.16 at d=2048, while FBMP is 0.34 and 0.40, respectively.
rows.note: This demonstrates that the paper's matching procedure can select coalitions of latents; it does not establish that each concept is represented by a single canonical latent.
rows.check: Compares the study's own FBMP against naive top-k matching; this is method performance.

relation.reason: The study reports its own concept-recovery and perturbation-alignment results, including incomplete recovery and configuration-dependent alignment.

tranche.reason: Annotated vision representations provide a new setting with results bearing on dictionary-feature completeness and dependence on configuration.

source_check.notes: TAPAScore measures responses to image edits, not effects of intervening on latents. Annotation quality and granularity bound the evaluation; feature canonicality and stability across training seeds are untested.

statements.correction: CLIP/CUB: coalitions outperform single-latent matching; all SAE variants remain below the supervised linear-probe bound. synCUB: perturbation-alignment evaluation. V5 verdict: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The matching and probe-bound findings are correct, but matching uses original CUB annotations, not synCUB. Incomplete recovery warrants limits_scope rather than challenges.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SAE concept matching and targeted perturbation tests on CLIP and DINOv2 vision encoders
reader_labels.reason: The findings are inconsistent with treating SAE features as complete, reliably causal concept units: multiple latents can be matched to one attribute, matching can improve while perturbation alignment worsens, and SAE matching remains below a supervised upper bound. The study does not test cross-run stability or canonicality. See r1–r8 and r11–r14.
